title: Game Programming & Design
description: Build in Unity. Understand the logic. Test your ideas.
alignmentNote: The six Essentials units follow Unity’s educator outline in mission order. Each is a classroom companion with original notes, a small C# exercise, Unity activities, and a checkpoint—not a replacement for every Unity Learn tutorial. Junior Programmer follows Essentials. Console exercises run separately from Unity scene scripts.

units.title: Editor Essentials
units.summary: Unity Essentials mission 1: navigate the Editor and compose a mural.

lessons.title: Find your way around a scene

sections.heading: Open the Essentials project
sections.text: Follow Unity Learn’s installation and project-opening tutorials before the Editor activities. Open the supplied Essentials project in the supported Editor version. In the Scene view, practice selecting, orbiting, panning, and zooming before arranging the mural. Save your work outside Play mode.

sections.heading: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Inspector
sections.text: The Scene view is your workspace for arranging a world. The Game view shows the view rendered by the game cameras. The Hierarchy lists GameObjects in the open scene; the Inspector shows the selected object’s components and settings. The Project window contains assets saved in the project.

sections.heading: Play mode is an experiment
sections.text: Save your scene, enter Play mode, change a value, then stop. Ordinary scene changes made during Play mode are not kept when you exit it. Make lasting edits outside Play mode. The Console shows messages, warnings, and errors; fix compilation errors before testing behavior.

sections.heading: Your first C# value
sections.text: A string is text inside double quotation marks. A declaration such as string label = "Arena"; stores a value in a named variable. C# statements usually end with a semicolon. In the provided Solution method, return hands one value back to the caller. Main is the console entry point; Console.WriteLine displays the returned value. Keep the provided class and method wrappers for now.

exercise.title: Name the practice arena
exercise.prompt: Inside Solution(), create a string variable named arenaName containing "Practice Arena". Return arenaName. Keep Main so you can see the result in a C# compiler.
hints: Use double quotes for the text.
Declare the string, then return the variable.

unityTask: Complete the installation and project-opening steps in the Unity Learn companion.
Complete the Scene-view navigation and flying-test activities.
Design the mural in the supplied scene. Save, enter Play mode, then stop and describe which edits persisted.

questions.prompt: Where do you inspect components on a selected GameObject?
questions.explanation: The Inspector displays components and their editable settings for the selection.

questions.prompt: Which view is used to arrange the world rather than see the camera output?
questions.explanation: Scene view is the editing workspace. Game view displays what the game cameras render.

questions.prompt: You move an ordinary scene object during Play mode, then stop. What should you normally expect?
choices: The change is saved to every scene
The edit is not retained after Play mode
The editor cannot exit Play mode
questions.explanation: Make lasting ordinary scene edits outside Play mode and save the scene.

questions.prompt: What does return do in the practice method?
choices: Sends a value back to its caller
questions.explanation: Returning a value and printing it are separate operations.

units.title: 3D Essentials
units.summary: Unity Essentials mission 2: furnish a room, test physics, and use prefab blocks.

lessons.title: GameObjects, components, and changing values

sections.heading: Objects are built from components
sections.text: A GameObject is a container. Its components provide behavior: Transform stores position, rotation, and scale; a Renderer displays geometry; a Collider defines a collision shape; a Rigidbody participates in physics simulation. A Collider alone does not make an object fall under gravity. A script can also be a component.

sections.heading: Choose a type for the job
sections.text: Use int for whole-number counts, float for decimal game quantities, bool for true or false, and string for text. Write a float literal with f, such as 2.5f. Assignment uses = and updates a variable. A method’s declared return type must match the value returned.

sections.heading: Move a coordinate in code
sections.text: Addition can update a coordinate: float nextX = x + distance;. x and distance are parameters supplied when the method is called. Their values can change for each call; use the parameters instead of hard-coding an example answer. In Unity the Transform has three axes; this exercise isolates one axis as a number.

exercise.title: Move a practice marker
exercise.prompt: Return x + distance as a float. Negative distances move in the opposite direction. Do not use UnityEngine in this console exercise.
hints: Both inputs already have the right numeric type.
Return an expression using both parameters.

unityTask: Arrange furniture in the supplied kid’s bedroom. Adjust Transform values outside Play mode.
Create a ball with a Collider and Rigidbody; test its bounce with a physics material.
Create a prefab block and build a tower from instances. Adjust the room’s lighting, background, and camera, then save and test.

lessons.title: Prefab instances and scoring arithmetic

sections.heading: Asset versus instance
sections.text: A prefab asset is a reusable template in the Project window. Dragging it into a scene creates an instance in the Hierarchy. An instance can have overrides; editing one instance does not automatically change every other copy. Apply overrides deliberately when you intend to update the asset.

sections.heading: Explain the scoring formula
sections.text: Multiplication happens before addition in score + coins * pointsPerCoin. The three int parameters let the same method score many situations. The method returns the new total; returning a value is different from displaying it. Main prints the returned value for testing.

exercise.title: Score a pickup batch
exercise.prompt: Return the existing score plus coins multiplied by pointsPerCoin. Inputs are nonnegative whole numbers. A batch of zero coins leaves the score unchanged.
exercise.signature: int Solution(int score, int coins, int pointsPerCoin)
hints: Calculate earned points from coins and pointsPerCoin.
Add earned points to the existing score.

unityTask: Compare a prefab asset with two instances in the scene.
Change an instance, then explain what changes when you edit the prefab asset instead.
Run the score rule for two different block counts and record the returned values.

questions.prompt: Which component makes a 3D object participate in physics simulation?
questions.explanation: A Rigidbody adds physics simulation; a Collider supplies a collision shape.

questions.prompt: What is a prefab asset?
questions.explanation: A prefab is a reusable template from which you can create instances.

units.title: Audio Essentials
units.summary: Unity Essentials mission 3: create and test an immersive soundscape.

lessons.title: Build a soundscape and adjust volume

sections.heading: Source and listener
sections.text: An AudioSource emits a clip; an AudioListener receives sound, commonly on the main camera. Import a clip, assign it to a source, and test Play On Awake and Loop deliberately. Avoid multiple active listeners.

sections.heading: 2D and 3D sound
sections.text: Spatial Blend controls whether sound behaves as 2D audio or depends on position in 3D. With 3D sound, test distance and volume while moving the listener. Use layered sounds in the kitchen scene, and keep levels comfortable.

sections.heading: Scale a numeric value
sections.text: Volume is a value from 0 to 1. For this console exercise, inputs already lie in that range. Multiplying volume by a gain from 0 to 1 makes it quieter. A float literal uses an f suffix, such as 0.5f. This arithmetic exercise returns a number; it does not play sound.

exercise.title: Build a soundscape and adjust volume
exercise.prompt: Return volume multiplied by gain. Inputs are between 0 and 1; no clamping is needed.
hints: Use the multiplication operator, *.
Return a numeric value rather than writing sound-playing code.

unityTask: Complete Create an immersive soundscape in the Unity Learn kitchen scene.
Use at least one looping sound and compare 2D with 3D spatial behavior.
Move the listener and explain how distance changes the sound.

questions.prompt: Which component emits audio?
questions.explanation: AudioSource emits sound; AudioListener receives it.

questions.prompt: What should you test for a 3D AudioSource?
questions.explanation: Spatial sound depends on the position of the source and listener.

units.title: Programming Essentials
units.summary: Unity Essentials mission 4: move a character, rotate an object, and collect it.

lessons.title: Scripts, methods, and a tiny game loop

sections.heading: Read the method contract
sections.text: public static int Solution(int score, int bonus) names a method, its inputs, and its returned type. The body between braces holds statements. A call such as Solution(10, 5) supplies arguments. A return sends the result back; Console.WriteLine prints it. This console wrapper does not inherit MonoBehaviour.

sections.heading: Understand Unity execution
sections.text: A Unity behavior typically inherits MonoBehaviour and is attached to a GameObject. Start runs once before that script’s first Update when it becomes enabled; Update runs each rendered frame while the behavior is active. Debug.Log writes to Unity’s Console. Console.WriteLine is for these standalone exercises. Do not paste the whole console Program into a Unity component.

sections.heading: Find the first useful error
sections.text: Read the first compiler error and its line number. A missing semicolon, wrong capitalization, or mismatched return type prevents compilation. A program can also compile but return the wrong value; try another input and explain the calculation. Fix one issue at a time.

sections.heading: Connect time to distance
sections.text: A speed of 6 units per second covers 3 units during 0.5 seconds. Multiplying speed by elapsed seconds makes the intended distance depend on elapsed time rather than on a count of frames. In a Unity Update method, Time.deltaTime supplies the elapsed seconds for the frame.

exercise.title: Calculate a frame’s travel distance
exercise.prompt: Return speed * elapsedSeconds. speed is units per second and elapsedSeconds is seconds. Both inputs are nonnegative. A paused interval of zero seconds produces zero distance.
hints: Keep both quantities in the same unit system.
Multiply; do not add speed and time.

unityTask: Complete Add a movement script in the supplied living room. Identify Start and Update.
Create a rotating collectible and test its motion.
Complete Collect the collectible. Add a Console message to confirm collection, then explain what the message tells you.

questions.prompt: Why multiply a speed by elapsed seconds?
choices: To calculate a distance for that interval
To convert a bool to text
To make every computer have the same frame rate
questions.explanation: Speed times elapsed time gives distance; it does not force a specific frame rate.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits Update in an active enabled MonoBehaviour?
choices: Once when the project is saved
questions.explanation: Update is a per-frame callback. Start is used for initial setup.

units.title: 2D Essentials
units.summary: Unity Essentials mission 5: build a 2D puzzle scene and animate a pet.

lessons.title: Work in a 2D scene

sections.heading: Sprites and the camera
sections.text: A SpriteRenderer displays a sprite. In a 2D scene, arrange objects in the XY plane and use an orthographic camera for a flat view. Sorting layers and order control which sprites appear in front; moving farther right changes x, not the sorting layer.

sections.heading: Use the 2D physics family
sections.text: Use Rigidbody2D and Collider2D components for 2D physics. They do not interact with the 3D Rigidbody and Collider family. Set up the puzzle room using the companion’s assets and instructions, then test its collisions.

sections.heading: Slice and animate
sections.text: The Sprite Editor can divide a sprite sheet into individual sprites. A sequence of frames forms an animation clip; an Animator plays clips according to its controller. Follow the animated-pet activity and inspect the clip frames.

sections.heading: Separate the movement rule
sections.text: The console practice uses arithmetic you have already learned. A horizontal offset adds to x; the unchanged y coordinate would still be handled separately in Unity. The console has no SpriteRenderer or Unity scene.

exercise.title: Work in a 2D scene
exercise.prompt: Return the new x coordinate after adding offset to x.
hints: Use addition.
Return x + offset.

unityTask: Complete Set up a 2D room and Complete your 2D Puzzle Game in the Unity companion.
Identify a SpriteRenderer, the camera, and a 2D physics component in your scene.
Complete Add an animated pet. Explain how frames, the animation clip, and Animator relate.

questions.prompt: Which pair belongs to the 2D physics system?
questions.explanation: Use the 2D component family together for 2D physics.

questions.prompt: What does a sprite animation clip contain?
questions.explanation: A sequence of sprite frames changes the displayed image over time.

units.title: Publishing Essentials
units.summary: Unity Essentials mission 6: build, test, document, and share your portfolio project.

lessons.title: Build, test, and share a project

sections.heading: A build is a separate test
sections.text: Saving a scene does not publish a game. A build packages the scenes and assets for a target platform. Include the intended scenes in the build list and test the starting scene. Follow the Unity companion for the build UI in your Editor version.

sections.heading: Test the web build
sections.text: Use the Web platform target (called WebGL in older versions). Test the built game through a web server or supported hosting service rather than opening its HTML as a local file. Check loading, controls, audio, and scene transitions. Editor success alone is not a build test.

sections.heading: Prepare portfolio evidence
sections.text: Complete the bonus scene, capture a short video, and share the project following classroom directions. Include controls, a description of what you made, and asset credits. Test the shared link on another device.

sections.heading: Create a short label
sections.text: In C#, + joins two strings. For example, "Game: " + title produces a label. This console exercise practices a readable project label; it does not build or upload a Unity project.

exercise.title: Build, test, and share a project
exercise.prompt: Return the text "Project: " followed by title. Include the space after the colon.
hints: Use + to join the prefix and title.
Return "Project: " + title.

unityTask: Complete Build your portfolio project and Publish to WebGL using the companion instructions for your Editor.
Complete the bonus-scene challenge and capture a video showing your game.
Share through the approved classroom destination. Verify the link, controls, and credits on another device.

questions.prompt: What is a necessary test before sharing a web build?
choices: Run the built version through supported hosting
questions.explanation: The packaged game must be tested separately from Editor Play mode.

questions.prompt: What should you check if your build opens the wrong scene?
choices: The included scenes and starting scene
questions.explanation: The build must include the intended scenes and start with the correct one.

units.title: Junior Programmer: player control & game rules
units.summary: Translate movement, boundaries, spawning permission, and life changes into testable C#.
units.pathway: Junior Programmer · Player Control / Basic Gameplay

lessons.title: Steer with inputs and frame time

sections.heading: Connect to Player Control
sections.text: Follow the Player Control mission in Unity Learn. Keep using the input approach shown by your assigned project: input APIs differ between project versions and input-system settings. The logic here accepts an already-read input value so the calculation remains the same.

sections.heading: Use a signed input
sections.text: An input of -1 means full movement in one direction, 0 means no movement, and 1 means full movement in the other. A value such as 0.5 represents partial input. Compute input * speed * elapsedSeconds, then add that displacement to the current position. Use float values and keep the f suffix on literal arguments.

sections.heading: Predict before you test
sections.text: If x is 5, input is -1, speed is 4, and time is 0.5, displacement is -2 and the next position is 3. This method models horizontal movement only. It does not set a Transform or apply a Rigidbody force.

exercise.title: Calculate the next player position
exercise.prompt: Return x + input * speed * elapsedSeconds. Input is between -1 and 1; speed and elapsedSeconds are nonnegative. Do not clamp the result in this lesson.
exercise.signature: float Solution(float x, float input, float speed, float elapsedSeconds)
hints: Compute displacement before adding the original position.
Preserve the sign of input.

unityTask: Follow Player Control and identify the variable controlling speed.
Predict the effect of doubling speed, test it, and restore the original value.
Explain why a camera needs a suitable position and viewing direction to show the player.

lessons.title: Keep a player inside the arena

sections.heading: A condition is a question
sections.text: The expressions x < min and x > max produce bool values. Use an if statement followed by a condition in parentheses and a body in braces. Return immediately when a condition identifies the required answer. == compares equality; = assigns a value.

sections.heading: Clamp means stop at the edge
sections.text: Clamping a position returns min when x is below min, max when x is above max, and x otherwise. At exactly min or max the value is already valid. Assume min <= max. This differs from wrapping to the other side or freezing before movement is calculated.

sections.heading: Test the boundaries
sections.text: Try below, inside, above, and exactly on an edge. Passing a normal input is not enough to show that boundary logic is correct. This lesson adds if statements to the numeric work already taught; no arrays or loops are required.

exercise.title: Clamp a player position
exercise.prompt: Return x clamped to the inclusive interval [min, max]. The bounds are valid and may be negative. Use comparisons and if statements; no Unity APIs are needed.
exercise.signature: float Solution(float x, float min, float max)
hints: Check the lower edge and upper edge separately.
If neither condition applies, return the original position.

unityTask: Add or locate the boundary checks in your Player Control project.
Test both edges and describe whether the project clamps, freezes, or removes an object.
Record a bug, the input that reveals it, and the change that fixes it.

lessons.title: Gate an action with game state

sections.heading: Connect to Basic Gameplay
sections.text: Follow the Basic Gameplay mission after Player Control. It introduces projectiles, prefab spawning, and collision decisions. A prefab is a template; Instantiate creates an instance at runtime. The C# exercise isolates the decision about whether spawning is allowed.

sections.heading: Combine conditions
sections.text: Use && when both conditions must be true, || when either is enough, and ! to reverse a bool. remaining <= 0f includes exactly zero. A rule can be written as a bool expression and returned directly. Parentheses make the intended grouping clear.

sections.heading: Keep one rule in one method
sections.text: A shot is allowed only when the fire button is pressed, the game is not over, and remaining cooldown is zero or below. The method returns permission; it does not spawn a projectile or reset the timer. Keeping the decision separate makes it easier to test.

exercise.title: Decide whether a player can fire
exercise.prompt: Return true only when pressed is true, gameOver is false, and remaining <= 0f. A negative remaining value is ready. Return a bool, not the text "true".
exercise.signature: bool Solution(bool pressed, bool gameOver, float remaining)
hints: All three conditions must be satisfied.
Use !gameOver to require the game to still be active.

unityTask: In Basic Gameplay, identify the prefab and the code that creates an instance.
Explain why spawning every Update without a gate would create many projectiles.
Describe how you would prevent shooting after game over.

lessons.title: Collisions, lives, and debugging a rule

sections.heading: Know which event you are expecting
sections.text: A Collider defines a shape. For typical 3D trigger events, colliders are involved, one is set as a trigger, and at least one object has an appropriate Rigidbody; layer settings and object state also affect whether events occur. A trigger detects overlap without physically blocking the other object. 2D physics uses its own components and callbacks.

sections.heading: Update lives once for one event
sections.text: Our exercise receives hit as an already-detected event. Start with nonnegative lives. If hit is true and lives > 0, return lives - 1; otherwise return lives unchanged. Combine conditions with &&. This is a pure rule: it does not configure physics or detect a collision.

sections.heading: Separate a rule from its side effects
sections.text: After receiving the new life count, Unity code could update UI and end the game when the count is zero. Keep these actions separate from the calculation. When a life disappears twice, inspect how many times the event handler ran before changing the subtraction.

sections.heading: Complete the small prototype
sections.text: Finish the Basic Gameplay practice assigned by your teacher. Demonstrate a moving player, a spawned prefab, an event that updates state, and a meaningful boundary. Explain a bug you found and how your test reveals that it is fixed.

exercise.title: Update remaining lives
exercise.prompt: Given nonnegative lives, subtract one only when hit is true and at least one life remains. Never return a negative value. If there is no hit, keep the value unchanged.
hints: Use && to combine a hit with having lives left.
Keep the existing lives in every other situation.

unityTask: Demonstrate one collision or trigger interaction in your prototype.
Explain whether that interaction should physically block the other object.
Test zero lives and explain how gameplay stops or changes state.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits Update in an active enabled MonoBehaviour?
choices: Once when the project is saved
questions.explanation: Update is a per-frame callback. Start is used for initial setup.

questions.prompt: A signed input of -1 usually represents what in our horizontal rule?
choices: Movement in the opposite direction from +1
questions.explanation: The negative sign reverses the displacement direction.

questions.prompt: A clamped player is exactly at the maximum boundary. What happens to that coordinate?
questions.explanation: Inclusive boundaries allow values exactly on either edge.

questions.prompt: Which operator compares two values for equality?
questions.explanation: == asks whether values are equal. = performs assignment.

questions.prompt: pressed is true, gameOver is false, and remaining is 0.2. Can our player fire?
choices: Yes, because the button is pressed
questions.explanation: All three requirements must be satisfied; remaining must be zero or below.

questions.prompt: What does instantiation do in the spawning workflow?
choices: Creates an instance from a template
questions.explanation: Instantiation creates an object instance at runtime.

questions.prompt: Why choose a trigger for a collectible?
choices: To detect overlap without physically blocking the player
questions.explanation: A trigger reports overlap instead of acting as an ordinary blocking collision surface.

questions.prompt: Lives decrease twice on one pickup. What is a useful first investigation?
choices: Count how often the event handler runs
questions.explanation: Repeated events can cause repeated state updates. Observe the calls before changing the rule.
